mcqs.question: In the monotonic deque invariant, why is it safe to permanently discard a trailing index whose value is less than or equal to the incoming value?
options: Because indices are always removed once their corresponding value turns negative
Because the deque is only allowed to hold a fixed maximum number of elements at once
Because that index has already been counted toward some earlier window's maximum
A later index with an equal-or-larger value stays valid at least as long and is at least as large, so the discarded index could never win a max comparison again while both remain candidates
mcqs.explanation: The new index dominates the discarded one on both axes that matter — it lasts at least as long in the window and its value is at least as large — so the discarded index is provably useless from that point forward. There's no capacity limit on the deque and no rule tied to sign; discarding is purely about future irrelevance.

mcqs.question: In the Sliding Window Maximum code, what does the check `if dq[0] <= i - k` accomplish?
options: It caps the deque so it never holds more than k elements total
It triggers popping the largest remaining value from the back of the deque
It expires the front index once it has aged out of the current width-k window, since the window's leftmost valid index is i - k + 1
It resets the entire deque whenever a new maximum value is encountered
mcqs.explanation: This check specifically handles the front of the deque falling outside the current window's left boundary — an entirely separate concern from the back-popping that maintains the decreasing-value order. It's not a capacity cap, and nothing about it resets the deque or targets the back.

mcqs.question: What actually breaks if the monotonic deque stores raw values instead of array indices?
options: The deque can no longer maintain a monotonically decreasing order of values
Popping from the back during a push becomes an O(n) operation instead of O(1)
The algorithm's overall time complexity increases from O(n) to O(n log n)
The front-expiry check becomes impossible, since a plain value carries no information about which position it came from — two equal values from different positions become indistinguishable
mcqs.explanation: The decreasing-order maintenance and the O(1) pop operations both still work fine with raw values — what specifically breaks is the ability to tell whether the front value has aged out of the window, since that check depends entirely on knowing a position, not just a value. The complexity class is unaffected either way.

mcqs.question: Why does the monotonic deque use less time and space than a max-heap for sliding window maximum?
options: Because heaps are structurally unable to store index information alongside a value
Because a max-heap requires the input array to be pre-sorted before use
The deque actively discards indices that can never become the max again, while a heap accumulates stale entries and only removes them lazily when they happen to surface at the top
Because deques are implemented with plain arrays while heaps require a linked structure
mcqs.explanation: The deque's eager back-popping keeps only genuinely useful candidates around at all times, bounding it to O(k) space and O(n) amortized time; a heap has no equivalent eager cleanup, so outdated entries linger until a pop happens to expose them, costing O(log k) per operation and up to O(n) space. Heaps can absolutely store (value, index) pairs, and neither structure requires a sorted input.
